KEY MESSAGE 1...
Cold frontal passage today will prompt shower and thunderstorm 
activity ahead and along the front with a good possibility of 
severe weather or at least stronger storms with the potential 
for damaging wind and heavy downpours. A pre- frontal trough 
will support the idea of energy along with dewpoints in the low 
70s and steep low level lapse rates to provide a corridor of 
strong surface based bouyancy ahead of storms. With a moist and 
destabilized warm sector to begin with, activity will likely be 
all day with the stronger thunderstorms ahead of the front this 
afternoon and lingering strong storms along the frontal boundary
later this afternoon and into the evening. 

Hi-res models have embedded thunderstorms in cluster waves 
ahead of the front and then a broken line along the front 
expected to trail into the area this late afternoon and into 
the evening when frontal passage is forecast to take place. Due 
to activity ahead of the front, the last bit of storm coverage 
may not be as strong as previous activity due to instability 
being used up with little in the way of the frontal boundary to 
work with, however this all depends on how much cloud coverage 
and activity we get in the late morning through the early to mid
afternoon.

With sufficient CAPE and robust shear updrafts will provide
stronger storms with the potential for downburst wind damage. 
We cannot rule out hail due to sufficient DCAPE and water loaded
sounding profiles which will be capable of bringing down hail 
fast enough to not melt all the way even with high freezing 
levels in place. Large hail will be hard to achieve but also we 
cannot rule out small hail and the possibility of a tornado or 
two. The significant tornado parameter is right at criteria 
along with lower LCLs and sufficient helicity, not too mention 
enough MUCAPE and no convective inhibition in place all to 
promote a slight potential tornadic environment. 

SPC has us in a slight risk to our eastern and northern flanks 
of our coverage area which will support higher instability and 
more scattered to widespread thunderstorm activity with 
stronger updrafts and downdrafts with the potential for hail 
and higher probability for tornadoes along with a higher threat
for damaging wind.

Heavy water loaded soundings with skinny CAPE and a very moist 
column with PWATS upwards near 2 to 3 standard deviations above 
the climatological norm will support downbursts along with 
heavy downpours which may cause localized flooding. The most 
prone areas ares ones that repeatedly get hit by heavy 
thunderstorm activity or even low lying and flood prone areas 
who get hit with 2+ inch per hour rates of heavy rain will be 
susceptible to localized flood issues. WPC has us in a marginal
threat for excessive rainfall for the entire area which support
isolated flooding chances, especially to the susceptible areas 
previously mentioned. 

Convective allowing models have broken segments of cluster 
storms along the aforementioned trough in front of the frontal 
boundary passing through in the afternoon. Timing on the 
activity will be much of the day, especially during peak 
heating hours a few hours prior to sunset as the frontal 
boundary pushes further into the region. A final line of 
embedded thunderstorms along a broken line will likely follow 
frontal passage until the evening at which point activity should 
wane by sunset.

The strongest storms will be across the eastern half of the 
coverage area as they progress up in the higher elevations 
with sufficient lift and stronger vertical velocities
such as steeper lapse rates supporting stronger updrafts and 
where wind where shear is ample enough to cause severe damaging
wind gusts.

After frontal passage and after all the expected storm activity
things will settle down as high pressure settles in at the 
surface and upper level zonal flow keeps the area settled into 
midweek with below seasonable temperatures expected to accompany
the settled weather. 

By mid day Wednesday, chances for precipitation come back to 
the region although much of the expected activity will be for 
Thursday as another could front is projected to impact the 
region with possible severe weather. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
A cold front is then expected to drive through on Thursday as
previously mentioned but some models have it hung up through 
Friday leaving high chances for precipitation and thunderstorm 
activity through that time frame. SPC currently has the area 
outlooked in a 15% risk for severe weather Thursday as a dynamic
mid-latitude cyclone approaches from the west. 

Models are showing the potential for strong shear and high CAPE
across the mid Ohio Valley and Appalachians with this system. 
Strong damaging wind will be a threat along with potential for 
other threats but precise aspects of this dynamic system will be
provided as time gets closer to the event.
